title: Perpetua and Felicity (203)
hook: a young noblewoman and her enslaved companion, whose own prison diary survives

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus, and God's glory in a human being fully alive. What did you do with your whole attention? Day seven hundred ten.

The darkness scared her. She had never known a place like it. The heat of the crowd, the soldiers shoving, and worst of all, worry for her baby. A young mother wrote that, in a prison in North Africa. Her name was Vibia Perpetua. She was well born, educated, married, nursing an infant son. Arrested with her was Felicity, an enslaved woman, heavily pregnant. They were catechumens, still preparing for baptism. And because Perpetua kept a record, we can hear her in her own words.
screen: `THE DARKNESS SCARED HER.` → `A PRISON IN NORTH AFRICA.` → `A MOTHER AND A MOTHER-TO-BE.`

segments.voice: The text is called the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity. First, her own hand. The narrator says that from here on, Perpetua tells the story herself, as she left it written with her own hand. A prisoner's notes, from the inside. Second, the baby. Deacons pay the guards so the prisoners can move to a better part of the jail for a few hours, and Perpetua nurses her son. When she's allowed to keep him with her, she writes that the prison suddenly felt like a palace. Her father comes again and again, begging her to give in for his sake and the child's. She grieves for him, and she doesn't give in. Third, Felicity. Pregnant women weren't put to death, and she's afraid she'll be held back while her friends die without her. Her companions pray with her, and she goes into labor. A guard sneers: if you cry out like this now, what will you do in front of the beasts? She answers: now I'm the one who suffers. Then another will be in me, who will suffer for me, because I'll be suffering for him. She gives birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman raises the girl as her own. Fourth, the arena. The text says Perpetua, thrown down, gets up, sees Felicity on the ground, and lifts her to her feet. The two stand together. Before they die, they give each other the kiss of peace. A noblewoman and an enslaved woman. At Mass, the first Eucharistic Prayer still names them both.
screen: `IN HER OWN HAND.` · `A BABY IN THE PRISON.` · `FELICITY GIVES BIRTH.` · `SHE LIFTS HER TO HER FEET.` · then, large: `THE KISS OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for young mothers. Settle, and breathe. Perpetua and Felicity were both new mothers, or nearly. Bring to mind a young mother you know: a friend, a sister, a neighbor, someone you saw on the bus with a stroller and a tired face. Think of the night feeds, the worry, the not knowing. Hold her there for a while. If you pray, you can ask God to give her rest and help. If you don't, simply wish her strength, and think of one practical thing you could offer this week. The bell holds the time.
passio. Latin for suffering, the word in the title of Perpetua's prison account, written partly in her own hand. Today's word.
Your line: sisters in the arena. Today, offer one young mother something practical: a meal, an hour, a message that says you're thinking of her. Day seven hundred ten.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Perpetua and Felicity as a memorial in the Church's calendar, and both are named among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.

notes: All of the Passion is paraphrased: the arrest of the catechumens (Felicity and Revocatus enslaved; Perpetua well born, educated, married, nursing a son); the narrator handing over to her own written account; the darkness, heat, crowding and soldiers; deacons Tertius and Pomponius paying for a better part of the prison; the prison 'became a palace'; the father's pleading; Felicity's fear of being delayed because she was pregnant, the companions' prayer, the guard's taunt and her answer, the daughter raised by a 'sister'; in the arena Perpetua rising and lifting Felicity; the kiss of peace.
